passages.title: The Bridge Builders
passages.text:
When the spring flood washed away the footbridge over Miller Creek, the kids on Elm Road lost their shortcut to school. Now the walk took twenty extra minutes along a busy road with no sidewalk.

“Someone should fix it,” said Jada, kicking a pebble into the muddy water.

“Someone like who?” her brother Eli asked. “The town says it'll take a year.”

Jada didn't answer. That night she sketched a design on graph paper: two sturdy logs, planks across the top, and rope railings. The next morning she showed it to Mr. Okafor, who ran the hardware store and had been an engineer.

He studied the drawing for a long time. “Your idea is good,” he said finally, “but the logs need to rest on solid rock, not mud. Otherwise the next flood will carry it away too.”

Jada's face fell. Then she noticed the boulders on the far bank. “What if we anchor it there?”

Mr. Okafor smiled. “Now you're thinking like an engineer.”

It took three weekends, eleven neighbors, and more blisters than Jada could count. Eli measured every plank twice. Mrs. Reyes brought lemonade. Even the town council member stopped by to check the safety of the railings.

On the first day of the new school year, Jada crossed the finished bridge and paused in the middle. Below her, the creek gurgled peacefully, as if it had forgiven them all.

passages.title: Tiny Plastics, Big Problem
passages.text:
Plastic does not simply disappear when it is thrown away. Over time, sunlight, wind, and waves break plastic bottles, bags, and wrappers into smaller and smaller pieces. Pieces smaller than five millimeters—about the size of a sesame seed—are called microplastics.

Microplastics have been found almost everywhere scientists have looked: in oceans, rivers, soil, and even on top of mountains. Some come from larger trash that breaks apart. Others are made small on purpose, such as the tiny beads once used in face scrubs. In the United States, a 2015 law banned these microbeads from rinse-off cosmetics.

Why are microplastics a concern? Many sea animals, from tiny plankton to large whales, mistake the pieces for food. When animals eat plastic, they may feel full without getting nutrients. In addition, plastic can absorb harmful chemicals from the water. Scientists are still studying how these chemicals move through food chains.

There are steps people can take. Using reusable water bottles and shopping bags reduces the amount of plastic that becomes trash. Picking up litter keeps plastic out of storm drains that lead to rivers and the ocean. Some cities are testing special filters that catch microplastics before water leaves treatment plants.

No single action will solve the problem. However, when millions of people make small changes, the amount of plastic reaching the environment can shrink.

passages.title: Second Chair
passages.text:
Amara had played first chair violin in the school orchestra for two years. First chair meant she sat closest to the conductor, played the solos, and tuned the other violins before every concert. So when the new seating chart was posted, she read it three times before she believed it.

First chair: Lucas Brennan. Second chair: Amara Osei.

Lucas had moved from Ohio in September. He was quiet and kept his violin case covered in stickers from national parks. Amara had barely spoken to him.

At rehearsal, she played every note louder than necessary. During the solo in the second movement, Lucas's bow trembled, and he lost his place. A few students snickered. Amara felt a flash of satisfaction—and then, almost immediately, a sting of guilt. She remembered her own first solo, when her hands shook so badly she nearly dropped her bow.

After rehearsal, she found Lucas packing up slowly. “The solo starts on the up-bow,” she said. “If you start on the down-bow, it throws off the whole phrase. I used to do it too.”

Lucas looked surprised. “Can you show me?”

They stayed twenty minutes after everyone left. By the concert, Lucas played the solo cleanly, and when the audience applauded, he turned and nodded toward the second chair.

Amara realized that her seat had changed, but her place in the orchestra had not.

passages.title: Why Sleep Matters for Students
passages.text:
Many students think of sleep as wasted time—hours that could be spent on homework, games, or friends. But scientists have found that sleep is one of the most important things the body and brain do.

While you sleep, your brain is busy. It sorts through information you learned during the day and stores important memories. In one study, students who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next day than students who stayed awake. Sleep also helps the body grow and repair muscles.

Doctors recommend that children ages 6 to 12 get 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours. However, surveys show that many students get much less. One major reason is screens. Phones, tablets, and computers give off blue light, which can trick the brain into thinking it is still daytime. This makes it harder to fall asleep.

Not getting enough sleep can cause problems. Tired students may have trouble paying attention, solving problems, and controlling their emotions. They may also get sick more often.

Fortunately, small habits can help. Going to bed at the same time every night trains the body's internal clock. Turning off screens an hour before bed and keeping the bedroom dark and cool also make sleep easier. A good night's rest is not wasted time; it is an investment in a better tomorrow.

passages.title: The Old Oak (a poem)
passages.text:
I stood here when the road was dirt,
When wagons creaked and horses snorted,
I watched the town grow brick by brick,
And every storm, my branches sorted.

The children climbed my knotted arms,
They carved their names, they swung from rope,
And when they left for distant towns,
I held their laughter, held their hope.

Now cars rush by in shining lines,
And towers rise where fields once lay,
But every spring I still unfold
My thousand leaves to greet the day.

So if you pass beneath my shade,
Remember those who came before—
I keep their stories in my rings,
And I will keep a hundred more.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a theme and how it is developed through details.
questions.question: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
choices: It is better to wait for the government to fix problems.
Floods are the most dangerous kind of weather.
A community can solve a problem when people combine ideas and effort.
Adults should always make decisions for children.
questions.correctAnswer: A community can solve a problem when people combine ideas and effort.
questions.explanation: Jada's idea, Mr. Okafor's expertise, and many neighbors' help build the bridge.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a character responds to challenges.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: How does Jada respond when Mr. Okafor points out a problem with her design?
choices: She argues that her plan is fine.
She asks Eli to build it alone.
She gives up on the idea.
She looks for a way to improve the plan.
correctAnswers: She looks for a way to improve the plan.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which sentence from the story best supports the answer to Part A?
choices: “Someone like who?” her brother Eli asked.
Then she noticed the boulders on the far bank. “What if we anchor it there?”
correctAnswers: Then she noticed the boulders on the far bank. “What if we anchor it there?”

questions.explanation: Although disappointed at first, Jada quickly proposes anchoring the bridge to the boulders.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including figurative language.
questions.question: What is the effect of the phrase “as if it had forgiven them all” in the last paragraph?
choices: It explains that the neighbors apologized to each other.
It suggests the bridge was built incorrectly.
It personifies the creek to show that the conflict with nature is resolved.
It shows that the creek is about to flood again.
questions.correctAnswer: It personifies the creek to show that the conflict with nature is resolved.
questions.explanation: Giving the creek human feelings suggests peace after the problem the flood caused.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Quote accurately from a text when drawing inferences.
questions.question: Select two details that show building the bridge required hard work from many people.
choices: Below her, the creek gurgled peacefully.
It took three weekends, eleven neighbors, and more blisters than Jada could count.
He studied the drawing for a long time.
Now the walk took twenty extra minutes along a busy road.
correctAnswers: It took three weekends, eleven neighbors, and more blisters than Jada could count.
Eli measured every plank twice.
questions.explanation: These details show time, effort, and many helpers.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Explain how a scene fits into the overall structure of a story.
questions.question: Why is the scene with Mr. Okafor important to the plot?
choices: It explains why the flood happened.
It shows that the bridge will never be built.
It introduces a problem with the design that leads to a stronger plan.
It is the moment the bridge is finished.
questions.correctAnswer: It introduces a problem with the design that leads to a stronger plan.
questions.explanation: His warning about mud leads Jada to anchor the bridge on rock.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Describe how a narrator's point of view influences how events are described.
questions.question: How does the third-person narrator help the reader understand Jada?
choices: The narrator speaks directly to the reader as Jada.
The narrator hides all of Jada's feelings.
The narrator only reports what Eli thinks.
The narrator describes Jada's actions and reactions, such as sketching the plan and her face falling.
questions.correctAnswer: The narrator describes Jada's actions and reactions, such as sketching the plan and her face falling.
questions.explanation: The narrator follows Jada closely, showing what she does and how she reacts.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a central idea and how it is conveyed through details.
questions.question: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: Microplastics are only found in the ocean.
Microplastics are widespread and harmful, but people can take steps to reduce them.
The 2015 law completely solved the microplastic problem.
Plankton and whales are the same size.
questions.correctAnswer: Microplastics are widespread and harmful, but people can take steps to reduce them.
questions.explanation: The passage explains what microplastics are, why they are a concern, and how people can help.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Trace and evaluate the argument and claims in a text.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: Which claim does the author support in paragraph 3?
choices: Microplastics are useful in face scrubs.
Microplastics can harm animals that eat them.
Microplastics only come from shopping bags.
Microplastics are larger than five millimeters.
correctAnswers: Microplastics can harm animals that eat them.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which two details best support the answer to Part A? Select two.
choices: Some come from larger trash that breaks apart.
In addition, plastic can absorb harmful chemicals from the water.
When animals eat plastic, they may feel full without getting nutrients.
Some cities are testing special filters.
Using reusable water bottles and shopping bags reduces the amount of plastic.
correctAnswers: When animals eat plastic, they may feel full without getting nutrients.
In addition, plastic can absorb harmful chemicals from the water.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that eating plastic replaces nutrients and may expose animals to chemicals.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
questions.question: In paragraph 3, what does the word absorb mean?
questions.explanation: Plastic can soak up harmful chemicals from the water.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a section fits into the overall structure of a text.
questions.question: How does paragraph 4 contribute to the passage?
choices: It presents solutions to the problem described earlier.
It describes the history of plastic.
questions.correctAnswer: It presents solutions to the problem described earlier.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists steps people and cities can take.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite textual evidence to support analysis.
questions.question: Select two places where the passage says microplastics have been found.
correctAnswers: in soil
on top of mountains
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists oceans, rivers, soil, and mountaintops.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine an author's point of view or purpose.
questions.question: What is the author's main purpose in the last paragraph?
choices: to explain how plastic is made
to entertain readers with a story about the ocean
to argue that the problem cannot be solved
to encourage readers that small actions by many people can make a difference
questions.correctAnswer: to encourage readers that small actions by many people can make a difference
questions.explanation: The author says millions of small changes can shrink the problem.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a theme and analyze its development.
questions.question: Which theme is developed in the story?
choices: Helping a rival can be more meaningful than holding on to a title.
New students should not join an orchestra.
Talent matters more than hard work.
questions.correctAnswer: Helping a rival can be more meaningful than holding on to a title.
questions.explanation: Amara chooses to help Lucas and discovers her value isn't tied to her chair.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a character's thoughts and actions reveal change.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: What causes Amara to change her attitude toward Lucas?
choices: She remembers how nervous she was during her own first solo.
The conductor tells her to help him.
She finds out Lucas is from Ohio.
She is moved back to first chair.
correctAnswers: She remembers how nervous she was during her own first solo.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which sentence from the story best supports the answer to Part A?
choices: She remembered her own first solo, when her hands shook so badly she nearly dropped her bow.
At rehearsal, she played every note louder than necessary.
Lucas had moved from Ohio in September.
correctAnswers: She remembered her own first solo, when her hands shook so badly she nearly dropped her bow.

questions.explanation: Amara's guilt comes from remembering her own nervous first solo.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
questions.question: In paragraph 4, what does the phrase “a sting of guilt” suggest about Amara?
choices: She was hurt by her violin strings.
She quickly feels bad about enjoying Lucas's mistake.
She is proud of her loud playing.
She is angry at the students who laughed.
questions.correctAnswer: She quickly feels bad about enjoying Lucas's mistake.
questions.explanation: “Sting” suggests a sudden, sharp feeling of regret.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite evidence to support inferences about characters.
questions.question: Select two details that show Amara was upset about the seating chart at first.
choices: He kept his violin case covered in stickers.
He turned and nodded toward the second chair.
She played every note louder than necessary.
She read it three times before she believed it.
They stayed twenty minutes after everyone left.
correctAnswers: She read it three times before she believed it.
She played every note louder than necessary.
questions.explanation: Both details show Amara's shock and frustration.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a sentence fits into the structure of a text and contributes to theme.
questions.question: How does the last sentence contribute to the story?
choices: It explains how orchestra seating works.
It introduces a new conflict with Lucas.
It hints that Amara will quit the orchestra.
It shows Amara understands that her value is not defined by her seat.
questions.correctAnswer: It shows Amara understands that her value is not defined by her seat.
questions.explanation: The final line states the lesson Amara learns.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a central idea and summarize the text.
questions.question: Which sentence best states the central idea of the passage?
choices: Homework should be done late at night.
Blue light from screens is the only cause of tiredness.
Teenagers need more sleep than children.
Sleep is important for learning and health, and good habits can help students get enough of it.
questions.correctAnswer: Sleep is important for learning and health, and good habits can help students get enough of it.
questions.explanation: The passage explains benefits of sleep, problems with too little sleep, and tips for better sleep.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a text explains cause and effect.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: According to the passage, how do screens affect sleep?
choices: Screens cause muscles to repair faster.
Blue light can make the brain think it is daytime, making it harder to fall asleep.
Screens make the bedroom too cold.
correctAnswers: Blue light can make the brain think it is daytime, making it harder to fall asleep.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which sentence best supports the answer to Part A?
choices: Phones, tablets, and computers give off blue light, which can trick the brain into thinking it is still daytime.
They may also get sick more often.
Sleep also helps the body grow and repair muscles.
correctAnswers: Phones, tablets, and computers give off blue light, which can trick the brain into thinking it is still daytime.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains the cause-and-effect relationship between blue light and falling asleep.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Evaluate how an author supports claims with evidence.
questions.question: Which evidence does the author use to support the claim that sleep helps memory?
choices: a study showing students who slept remembered more words
a survey about how many hours teenagers sleep
questions.correctAnswer: a study showing students who slept remembered more words
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the word-list study.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine figurative and connotative meanings of words.
questions.question: What does the author mean by calling sleep “an investment in a better tomorrow”?
choices: Sleep should be saved for the weekend.
Tomorrow will always be better than today.
Students should pay money for sleep.
Sleeping well now leads to benefits later.
questions.correctAnswer: Sleeping well now leads to benefits later.
questions.explanation: An investment is something you put effort into now for a future benefit.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite textual evidence.
questions.question: Select two habits the passage recommends for better sleep.
choices: going to bed at the same time every night
drinking a sports drink before bed
turning off screens an hour before bed
keeping the bedroom bright and warm
correctAnswers: going to bed at the same time every night
turning off screens an hour before bed
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 lists a consistent bedtime, no screens, and a dark, cool room.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a paragraph contributes to the development of ideas.
questions.question: How does the first paragraph introduce the topic?
choices: It presents a common belief about sleep and then challenges it.
It tells a story about a student who fell asleep in class.
It compares sleep in humans and animals.
It lists the steps for falling asleep.
questions.correctAnswer: It presents a common belief about sleep and then challenges it.
questions.explanation: It mentions sleep as “wasted time” and then says scientists disagree.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the theme of a poem.
questions.question: What is the theme of the poem?
choices: Cities should not build towers near trees.
Storms are the greatest danger to old trees.
Nature can connect the past and the present by holding memories over time.
questions.correctAnswer: Nature can connect the past and the present by holding memories over time.
questions.explanation: The oak remembers generations and keeps their stories in its rings.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the meaning of figurative language in a poem.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: Which literary device is used throughout the poem?
choices: onomatopoeia, because the poem is full of sound words
personification, because the tree speaks and remembers
alliteration, because every line starts with the same sound
hyperbole, because the tree is described as huge
correctAnswers: personification, because the tree speaks and remembers

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which line best supports the answer to Part A?
choices: And towers rise where fields once lay,
Now cars rush by in shining lines,
I held their laughter, held their hope.
When wagons creaked and horses snorted,
correctAnswers: I held their laughter, held their hope.

questions.explanation: The tree speaks as “I” and holds human feelings like laughter and hope.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Explain how stanzas fit together to provide structure.
questions.question: How does the third stanza differ from the first stanza?
choices: The first stanza rhymes, and the third does not.
The first stanza is spoken by a child, and the third is spoken by the tree.
The first stanza describes the town's past, and the third describes the present.
The first stanza is about children, and the third is about storms.
questions.correctAnswer: The first stanza describes the town's past, and the third describes the present.
questions.explanation: Stanza 1 mentions dirt roads and wagons; stanza 3 mentions cars and towers.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as used in a text.
questions.question: What does “I keep their stories in my rings” most likely mean?
choices: The tree's growth over the years holds the memories of the people who lived nearby.
The tree has forgotten everyone who visited.
The tree writes stories on paper.
The tree wears rings on its branches.
questions.correctAnswer: The tree's growth over the years holds the memories of the people who lived nearby.
questions.explanation: Tree rings mark years of growth, so the line connects years with memories.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use evidence to support an analysis of a poem.
questions.question: Select two lines that show how the town has changed over time.
choices: My thousand leaves to greet the day.
And towers rise where fields once lay,
So if you pass beneath my shade,
The children climbed my knotted arms,
Now cars rush by in shining lines,
correctAnswers: Now cars rush by in shining lines,
And towers rise where fields once lay,
questions.explanation: These lines contrast modern cars and towers with the earlier fields.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Form and use the perfect verb tenses.
questions.question:
Which words correctly complete the sentence?

By the time we arrived at the theater, the movie ___ .
questions.explanation: The past perfect (had + past participle) shows an action finished before another past action.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use correlative conjunctions.
questions.question: Which sentence uses correlative conjunctions correctly?
choices: Either the coach nor the players wanted to cancel the game.
Both the coach or the players wanted to cancel the game.
Neither the coach nor the players wanted to cancel the game.
Neither the coach or the players wanted to cancel the game.
questions.correctAnswer: Neither the coach nor the players wanted to cancel the game.
questions.explanation: “Neither” pairs with “nor.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use a comma to separate an introductory element.
questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: After the long hike, we rested by the lake.
After the long, hike we rested by the lake.
After the long hike we, rested by the lake.
After, the long hike we rested by the lake.
questions.correctAnswer: After the long hike, we rested by the lake.
questions.explanation: Use a comma after an introductory phrase.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works.
questions.question: Which sentence shows the titles written correctly?
choices: We read the poem The Road Not Taken in the book “Classic Poems.”
We read the poem “The Road Not Taken” in the book “Classic Poems.”
We read the poem “The Road Not Taken” in the book Classic Poems.
We read the poem The Road Not Taken in the book Classic Poems.
questions.correctAnswer: We read the poem “The Road Not Taken” in the book Classic Poems.
questions.explanation: Short works like poems go in quotation marks; long works like books are italicized or underlined.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense.
questions.question: Which sentence has a correct, consistent verb tense?
choices: Leo opens the door and walked into the kitchen.
Leo opened the door and walks into the kitchen.
Leo will open the door and walked into the kitchen.
Leo opened the door and walked into the kitchen.
questions.correctAnswer: Leo opened the door and walked into the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Both verbs should be in the past tense.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use interjections and a comma to set off yes and no.
questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: Yes, I finished my science project.
Yes I finished my science project,
Yes I finished, my science project.
Yes I, finished my science project.
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, I finished my science project.
questions.explanation: Use a comma after “yes” or “no” at the start of a sentence.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Interpret similes and metaphors in context.
questions.question:
What does the simile mean?

After recess, the classroom was as quiet as a library.
choices: The classroom was full of books.
questions.explanation: A simile compares two things using “like” or “as.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Explain the meaning of common idioms.
questions.question:
What does the idiom mean?

Dad said the new video game cost an arm and a leg.
choices: The game was about a robot.
Dad hurt himself playing the game.
The game was easy to play.
questions.explanation: “Cost an arm and a leg” means something is very expensive.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Explain the meaning of common idioms.
questions.question:
What does the idiom mean?

Lena was feeling under the weather, so she stayed home.
choices: She was hiding under a blanket.
She was standing in the rain.
She was excited about a storm.
questions.explanation: “Under the weather” means feeling ill.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Interpret figurative language, including personification.
questions.question: Which sentence uses personification?
choices: The wind whispered through the tall grass.
The wind was cold and strong.
The grass was as tall as a fence.
The tall grass swayed in the wind.
questions.correctAnswer: The wind whispered through the tall grass.
questions.explanation: Personification gives human qualities (whispering) to something that is not human.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Interpret figurative language, including hyperbole.
questions.question: Which sentence is an example of hyperbole?
choices: I have told you twice to clean your room.
Your room is like a jungle.
I have told you a million times to clean your room.
questions.correctAnswer: I have told you a million times to clean your room.
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is an extreme exaggeration.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use the relationship between words (synonyms, antonyms) to understand each.
questions.question: Which word is an antonym of generous?
questions.explanation: An antonym has the opposite meaning; generous means willing to give.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unknown word.
questions.question:
Read the sentence.

The scientist made a hypothesis, or educated guess, about why the plants grew faster.

What does the word hypothesis mean?
questions.explanation: Clues in the sentence show that “hypothesis” means “an educated guess.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unknown word.
questions.question:
Read the sentence.

The flood caused extensive damage; nearly every street in town needed repairs.

What does the word extensive mean?
questions.explanation: Clues in the sentence show that “extensive” means “large in amount or area.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unknown word.
questions.question:
Read the sentence.

Unlike his gregarious sister, who loved parties, Sam preferred to spend time alone.

What does the word gregarious mean?
questions.explanation: Clues in the sentence show that “gregarious” means “enjoying the company of others.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unknown word.
questions.question:
Read the sentence.

The instructions were ambiguous, so half the class built the model one way and half built it another.

What does the word ambiguous mean?
choices: unclear; open to more than one meaning
questions.correctAnswer: unclear; open to more than one meaning
questions.explanation: Clues in the sentence show that “ambiguous” means “unclear; open to more than one meaning.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unknown word.
questions.question:
Read the sentence.

The artist used vivid colors, like bright orange and electric blue, in her mural.

What does the word vivid mean?
questions.explanation: Clues in the sentence show that “vivid” means “bright and strong.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use common affixes as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The affix over- means “too much.” What does the word overcook mean?
questions.explanation: over- means “too much,” so overcook means “cook too much.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use common affixes as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The affix non- means “not.” What does the word nonfiction mean?
choices: writing that is not made up
questions.correctAnswer: writing that is not made up
questions.explanation: non- means “not,” so nonfiction means “writing that is not made up.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use common affixes as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The affix -ness means “state of being.” What does the word kindness mean?
questions.explanation: -ness means “state of being,” so kindness means “the state of being kind.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use common affixes as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The affix im- means “not.” What does the word impossible mean?
questions.explanation: im- means “not,” so impossible means “not possible.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use common affixes as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The affix inter- means “between.” What does the word international mean?
questions.explanation: inter- means “between,” so international means “between nations.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use common affixes as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The affix trans- means “across.” What does the word transatlantic mean?
questions.explanation: trans- means “across,” so transatlantic means “across the Atlantic.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use Greek or Latin roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The root graph means “write.” What does the word autograph most likely mean?
questions.explanation: The root graph (“write”) helps show that autograph means “a person's own signature.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use Greek or Latin roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The root tele means “far.” What does the word telescope most likely mean?
choices: a tool for seeing things far away
questions.correctAnswer: a tool for seeing things far away
questions.explanation: The root tele (“far”) helps show that telescope means “a tool for seeing things far away.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use Greek or Latin roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The root port means “carry.” What does the word portable most likely mean?
questions.explanation: The root port (“carry”) helps show that portable means “able to be carried.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use Greek or Latin roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The root aud means “hear.” What does the word audible most likely mean?
questions.explanation: The root aud (“hear”) helps show that audible means “able to be heard.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use Greek or Latin roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The root spect means “look.” What does the word spectator most likely mean?
choices: a person who plays in an event
a person who watches an event
questions.correctAnswer: a person who watches an event
questions.explanation: The root spect (“look”) helps show that spectator means “a person who watches an event.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use Greek or Latin roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
questions.question: The root bio means “life.” What does the word biology most likely mean?
questions.explanation: The root bio (“life”) helps show that biology means “the study of living things.”
